clue.text: Outstanding rule about dead fascist, as his friends called him?

definitions.text: fascist, as his friends called him?

indicators.note: 'about' can mean turned round, so the word for rule is read from its end back to its start

blocks.note: o/s is the accounting abbreviation for an outstanding balance
a law is a rule
d is the standard abbreviation for dead, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: Someone wonders what pet name a dead fascist's cronies used for him.
explanation.walkthrough: OS + WAL + D gives OSWALD, first name of Sir Oswald Mosley, leader of the British Union of Fascists. The question mark is fair: his friends in fact called him Tom.
explanation.definitionFit: Friends would use a first name, and Mosley's given forename was the one in the answer, though intimates actually preferred a nickname.

clue.text: School cane, a stinger, wielded across Charlie, a paradoxical creature

indicators.note: a stinger being wielded is swung about, so its letters are thrown into a new order
'across' says the jumbled letters stretch over and around the single letter for Charlie

blocks.note: SCH is the standard abbreviation for school
a cane used for punishment is a rod
the letters to be rearranged
Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A schoolmaster's cane is swung like a weapon at some unfortunate pupil.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram is only of 'a stinger'; school and cane are straight abbreviation and synonym placed before it. Schrödinger's cat is a thought experiment in quantum physics.
explanation.definitionFit: The physicist's thought experiment imagines a boxed animal simultaneously alive and dead, a famous quantum paradox.

clue.text: Old soldiers have twinges crossing two rivers

indicators.note: the twinges cross over each river, so the river letters end up placed within that word

blocks.note: twinges of pain are aches
R is the map abbreviation for river, taken twice

explanation.surface: Veterans complain of aches while wading across a couple of streams.
explanation.walkthrough: The two rivers do not go in together: each letter is slotted into a different gap in the twinges word.
explanation.definitionFit: Bowmen formed a key part of medieval armies, so they are soldiers of an earlier age.

clue.text: Comic part performed for three-ha’pence once

indicators.note: a part performed is worked through and acted out, so its letters are reworked into new order

blocks.note: The Dandy was a long-running British children's comic
the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An actor takes a comic role for a pitifully small fee in olden days.
explanation.walkthrough: DANDY + PRAT. Three-ha'pence means three halfpennies, a sum in pre-decimal British money.
explanation.definitionFit: A dandiprat was an old English coin worth one and a half pence, historically minted under Henry VII.

clue.text: Intellectual rebel has accident with car

indicators.note: an accident leaves things smashed and jumbled, so these letters come out in a wrecked new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A thoughtful rebel crashes their car.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone or something concerned with the mind and reasoning rather than feeling.

clue.text: Won everything when up, having lost everything when out

blocks.note: first meaning: followed by 'up', the phrase means scooped every prize
second meaning: followed by 'out', the phrase means left penniless

explanation.walkthrough: The same past tense takes opposite meanings depending on the small word after it: CLEANED UP versus CLEANED OUT.
explanation.definitionFit: To clean up is to win big; to be cleaned out is to lose all your money, both informal idioms.

clue.text: A survey run, and behold!

blocks.note: R is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for a run
ecce is Latin for behold, as in 'ecce homo'

explanation.surface: Someone does a quick survey, a run round, and exclaims at what they find.
explanation.walkthrough: R + ECCE.
explanation.definitionFit: A recce is informal British shorthand for reconnaissance, an exploratory inspection of ground before acting.

clue.text: Use live computer image of suspect with name attached

indicators.note: 'with' adds what follows directly onto what precedes it

blocks.note: to be is to live or exist
N is the abbreviation for name
an E-fit is a police likeness of a suspect assembled on a computer

explanation.surface: Police make use of a live digital picture of a suspect with a name on it.
explanation.walkthrough: The name goes before the image, not after it, despite 'attached'. E-fit is the British police term for an identikit picture.
explanation.definitionFit: As nouns, use and benefit both mean the advantage or good obtained from something.

clue.text: That’s a threat of retaliation in chess, for example

blocks.note: first meaning: a stock warning that you will hit back with the same tactics
second meaning: a pastime for exactly a pair of players

explanation.walkthrough: Chess is literally a contest for a pair of players, so the idiom of retaliation also describes it word for word.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom warns an opponent that you can use their tactics too; read literally it describes any two-player contest.

clue.text: Almost deceived at tea dance

indicators.note: 'almost' means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
'at' places one piece right beside the other

blocks.note: cha (or char) is British slang for tea
to be conned is to be deceived

explanation.surface: Someone is nearly swindled at a tea dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tea dance' looks like one phrase, but tea is wordplay and dance alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The chaconne is a stately baroque dance in triple time, later a musical form built on a repeated bass.

clue.text: Against epithet for the four Beatles in private conversation

blocks.note: con means against, as in pros and cons
the Beatles were nicknamed the Fab Four

explanation.surface: Someone opposes the nickname given to the Beatles in a private chat.
explanation.walkthrough: CON + FAB.
explanation.definitionFit: A confab, short for confabulation, is an informal chat or discussion between a few people.

clue.text: Bird entered the water the far side of the pond

definitions.text: entered the water the far side of the pond

blocks.note: first meaning: a pigeon-like bird, symbol of peace

blocks.clueFragment: entered the water the far side of the pond
blocks.note: second meaning: the American past tense of dive

explanation.walkthrough: 'The pond' is the Atlantic, so its far side, from Britain, is America, where the past of dive differs from British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun is a familiar small pigeon; in American English the same spelling serves as a past form of plunge-diving.

clue.text: Nursing a broken knee, turn to worship now in American style

indicators.note: to nurse is to hold close, so one piece cradles the other inside it
something broken is in pieces, so these letters are reassembled in a different order
'turn' tells us to flip the word for worship round from end to start

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, joined to the article as letters to rearrange
to deify is to worship as a god

explanation.surface: An injured patient nursing a damaged knee turns to prayer.
explanation.walkthrough: The worship word is turned round first, and then it wraps the jumbled letters after its opening Y. 'Now' marks the word as a modern coinage.
explanation.definitionFit: To be Yankeefied is to have been made thoroughly American in manner, Yankee being slang for a US citizen.

clue.text: One greeting king is servile, not unpleasant

indicators.note: 'not' tells us to take away a word meaning unpleasant from the word before it

blocks.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king
taken as written
the word to be cut down; vile means unpleasant

explanation.surface: A courtier greets the king with a fawning manner that is not unwelcome.
explanation.walkthrough: SERVILE without VILE leaves SER, so K + IS + SER.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who greets with a peck on the cheek is literally a kisser, an agent noun from the verb.

clue.text: The centre of Bangor?

blocks.note: surface reading: the middle of a town in Wales or Northern Ireland
setter's reading: the Northern Ireland Bangor is a seaside town in County Down, so it is a town of that county

explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as two words: Bangor is a Down town, being in County Down, and the whole word also means a town centre.
explanation.definitionFit: The American term for a city's central commercial district matches the centre of any town.

clue.text: Sleepers in monastery abroad losing pants

indicators.note: 'in' here signals that one piece is placed inside another
pants is British slang for rubbish, so the preceding word is rendered a mess

blocks.note: a wat is a Buddhist monastery or temple in Thailand or Cambodia
the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Monks in a foreign monastery sleep after losing their trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Losing' looks like a deletion signal but is the anagram fodder. In British slang pants means rubbish, and also underwear.
explanation.definitionFit: Wagons-lits are French railway sleeping cars, as run on the Orient Express, so they are sleepers.

clue.text: Costing a bomb to be sceptical

indicators.note: a bomb blows things apart, so these letters land in a scattered new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, joining the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Being sceptical about something that costs a fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Costing a bomb' is British slang for very expensive, but here the article joins the fodder and the bomb blows it all apart.
explanation.definitionFit: An agnostic doubts or withholds belief, especially about God, so the word fits a sceptical stance.

clue.text: Old bridge, not a tube

indicators.note: 'not a' tells us to remove one letter A from the word for bridge

blocks.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old
a viaduct is a long bridge carrying a road or railway

explanation.surface: An old bridge is described as being something other than a pipe.
explanation.walkthrough: O + VIADUCT without its A.
explanation.definitionFit: The oviduct is the passage carrying eggs from ovary to womb, an anatomical duct or channel.

clue.text: Start to cultivate non-native tree, its heart extracted for coffee substitute

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept
the heart is the middle letter, and extracting it removes it from the tree's name

blocks.note: the opening letter of cultivate
the hickory is a North American nut tree, not native to Britain

explanation.surface: Gardening advice: grow a foreign tree, then pull out its core to make ersatz coffee.
explanation.walkthrough: HICKORY has seven letters, so its central fourth letter K goes: C + HICORY.
explanation.definitionFit: Roasted, ground root of the chicory plant has long been brewed as a cheap stand-in or additive for real coffee.

clue.text: I stole Christmas, and grimace at church

blocks.note: a grin is a broad facial expression, a kind of grimace
CH is the standard abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: A confession of a Christmas theft, followed by pulling a face at church.
explanation.walkthrough: GRIN + CH.
explanation.definitionFit: Dr Seuss's book How the Grinch Stole Christmas makes its green villain the thief of the holiday.

clue.text: Introduce oxygen, burning part of church

blocks.note: a fire that is still in is burning
a spire is the tapering top of a church tower

explanation.surface: Feeding oxygen to a fire that has caught part of a church.
explanation.walkthrough: IN + SPIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: In its physiological sense, to inspire is to breathe in, drawing air and its oxygen into the lungs.

clue.text: Clamour interrupts lengthy sermon for special service

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break into the middle, so the noise sits inside the speech

blocks.note: an oration is a long formal speech
a din is a loud clamour

explanation.surface: Noise breaks into a long-winded sermon at a special church service.
explanation.walkthrough: The clamour goes in after the first two letters of the speech.
explanation.definitionFit: The ceremony making someone a priest or minister is a particular religious rite held in church.

clue.text: Ring area of the kidneys, not large

indicators.note: 'not large' tells us to drop the letter standing for large, as on clothing sizes

blocks.note: A is the abbreviation for area
renal means relating to the kidneys

explanation.surface: Medical jargon about a ring-shaped area of the kidneys.
explanation.walkthrough: A + RENAL without its L.
explanation.definitionFit: A boxing or circus ring is an enclosed space for contests or shows, which is what an arena is.

clue.text: Start off speaking with grit

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that is taken

blocks.note: the opening letter of speaking
and means along with

explanation.surface: Someone begins a speech with determination.
explanation.walkthrough: S + AND. 'Start off' looks like begin, but it marks the first letter of the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: Grit is small loose particles of stone, essentially coarse sand.

clue.text: Charge a line of waiters has announced

indicators.note: something announced is spoken out, so we go by how the words sound

blocks.note: a queue is a line of people waiting, and queue's is short for queue has

explanation.surface: A restaurant manager announces a charge against a row of waiting staff.
explanation.walkthrough: The waiters are not restaurant staff but people waiting in a queue; 'has' becomes the contracted 's.
explanation.definitionFit: To charge someone with an offence is formally to blame or indict them, which is to accuse.

clue.text: Call to attention fifty competitors that may be drilled

blocks.note: oi is a shout to get someone's attention
L is the Roman numeral for fifty
the field is all the competitors in a race

explanation.surface: A sergeant calls fifty recruits to attention for drill practice.
explanation.walkthrough: OI + L + FIELD. 'Drilled' suggests military parade drill, but means boring for petroleum.
explanation.definitionFit: An area with underground petroleum reserves is where wells are bored, so it is something drilled into.

clue.text: Figures and a piece of data applied to the rest of Jan

indicators.note: the rest is what remains once the named part is taken away from the whole word

blocks.note: a stat is a single statistic
Jan is short for the month, so the full name minus those three letters is wanted

explanation.surface: Figures from a set of statistics are applied to the remainder of January.
explanation.walkthrough: STAT + UARY, the last four letters of the month once its abbreviation is removed. 'Figures' suggests numbers but means sculptures.
explanation.definitionFit: Statuary is a collective noun for sculpted figures, such as statues placed in a garden.

clue.text: Under compulsion, you make irregular patterns

blocks.note: someone tied is bound by obligation
ye is the old form of you

explanation.surface: Someone is forced to produce irregular designs.
explanation.walkthrough: TIED + YE.
explanation.definitionFit: Tie-dyeing knots fabric before dyeing it, so the colour takes unevenly and forms random blotchy designs.
